notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 115, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Introduction and Structure

Psalm 115 is part of the Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113–118), sung by Jews at Passover — which means it was sung by Jesus and His disciples on the night before His crucifixion (Matt. 26:30; Mark 14:26). Most commentators agree it is liturgical, composed for alternating voices in temple worship: the congregation, priests, and Levites would each sing assigned parts. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/115.htm

Ellicott notes that the psalm has a historic interest for Englishmen, having been chanted by order of Henry V after the battle of Agincourt. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/115.htm

Spurgeon divides it: an entreaty for God to vindicate His honour (vv. 1–2); a contemptuous description of false gods (vv. 3–8); an exhortation to trust God and expect blessing (vv. 9–15); an explanation of God’s relationship to the present condition (v. 16); and a reminder that the living, not the dead, must praise God (vv. 17–18). — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

---

## Verse 1

**“Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, because of Your loving devotion, because of Your faithfulness.”**

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist opens with a fervent rejection of all self-glory. When God does wonderful things, the glory belongs to God alone, not to His people, even if they were active in the work. The repetition (“not to us… not to us”) shows vehemence — they loathe the idea of seeking their own glory. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/ ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

Spurgeon says the prayer is “tinctured with a consciousness of unworthiness”; because of past unfaithfulness the people hardly dare appeal to the covenant for their own sake, so they fall back on the honour of God’s name — the same argument Moses used (“Wherefore should the Egyptians speak…?”) and Joshua (“What wilt thou do unto thy great name?”). — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

Gill explains that no glory is due to men — not for their being, preservation, or any mercy of life, nor for spiritual blessings like election, redemption, or sanctification. All glory belongs to the Lord. The Targum renders it: “Not for our sakes, O Lord, not for our merit, but to thy name give glory.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

Guzik notes that “mercy” translates the Hebrew *hesed* — Yahweh’s covenant love, His loyal love. John 1:17 (“grace and truth came through Jesus Christ”) echoes the same idea and sees it fulfilled in Jesus. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Spurgeon records that Adoniram Judson, the missionary, was full of ambition until he met this text: “all his bright visions for the future seemed to vanish as these words sounded in his soul, ‘Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory.’” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

**Differing nuance — Pulpit Commentary:** The verse is a prayer that God help Israel — but not for their sakes, not to cover them with glory, rather for His own Name’s sake, so that glory may rest on His Name among the nations. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

---

## Verse 2

**“Why should the nations say, ‘Where is their God?’”**

**Traditional reading:** This is a skillfully formed, subtle prayer. The psalmist asks God to deliver His people so that the nations have no grounds to scoff. The taunt arose because Israel’s God was invisible — no outward emblem or image — whereas the heathen had visible, tangible idols. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/ ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

Spurgeon elaborates: when the godly are downtrodden while the wicked live at ease, the wicked multiply taunts and argue that their irreligion is better than faith. “This is the very sting of the trials of God’s chosen” — to see God’s name profaned because of their sufferings. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Ellicott:** The idolater who could point to his deity felt an apparent triumph over the worshipper of the invisible God when outward events went against the latter. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/115.htm

---

## Verse 3

**“Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases.”**

**Traditional reading:** At best, nations worshipped imaginary beings or projections of their own lusts; at worst, demonic spirits. Yahweh is different: He lives and reigns in heaven and does whatever He pleases — sovereign over all. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Spurgeon: “Where he should be; above the reach of mortal sneers … Supreme above all opposing powers … absolute in will and infinite in power.” God does not work miracles “at the beck and call of every vainglorious boaster.” Even Pharaoh was but clay on the potter’s wheel, and God’s purposes were fully answered in him. — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Gill:** God dwells in the highest heaven, overlooks all persons and things on earth, and overrules all. He does what He pleases in creation, providence, and grace — saves and calls people not according to their works, but according to His own purpose and will. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

**Reformed emphasis:** Both Spurgeon and Gill draw out the strong sovereignty theme here — God’s absolute freedom and power, echoing the Reformed understanding of divine sovereignty.

---

## Verses 4–7

**“Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men. They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see; they have ears, but cannot hear; they have noses, but cannot smell; they have hands, but cannot feel; they have feet, but cannot walk; they cannot even clear their throats.”**

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist exposes the folly of idolatry with sharp, almost humorous sarcasm. Men worship statues of precious metal that they themselves made — fashioned with human body parts (mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands, feet, throat), yet utterly unable to use them. Men worship things “demonstrably beneath themselves.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

The Pulpit Commentary notes: the inspired writers felt that when idolatry came under consideration, the criticism should be “brief and trenchant.” The satire here is imitated in Psalm 135:15–18 and echoed in Isaiah 44:9–20. Even idols of the Babylonians were of precious materials (gold and silver), but still merely the work of men’s hands. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

Spurgeon’s vivid remarks: “A god who has eyes, and cannot see, is a blind deity; and blindness is a calamity, and not an attribute of godhead. He must be very blind who worships a blind god.” On the nose: “In sacred scorn he mocks at those who burn sweet spices … offered to an image whose nose cannot perceive the perfume.” On the feet: “The meanest insect has more power of locomotion than the greatest heathen god.” — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Gill:** Notes that the idol of Jupiter at Crete was actually made without ears, because it was thought unbecoming that the prince and lord of all should give ear to any. On “neither speak they through their throat”: the Hebrew word implies not even an inarticulate sound like a bird’s chirp or a dove’s mournful coo (cf. Isa. 38:14), much less articulate speech. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

**Ellicott:** The passage “cannot compare with the magnificent irony of Isaiah 44:9–20,” but still has a noticeable vein of sarcasm, even more visible in the original Hebrew than in English. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/115.htm

---

## Verse 8

**“Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them.”**

**Traditional reading:** This is virtually a spiritual law: we become like what we worship. When people worship things beneath them, it brings them lower — they lose their own capacity to perceive and interact with the world. False gods always drag men down, never up. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Maclaren (cited by Guzik): “Worship is sure to breed likeness. A lustful, cruel god will make his devotees so. Men make gods after their own image, and, when made, the gods make men after theirs. The same principle which degrades the idolater lifts the Christian to the likeness of Christ.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

F.B. Meyer (cited by Guzik): “Men first impute to their deities their own vices … and then endeavour to honour them by imitation.” Positively, “This is the Divine method: look and live; trust and be transfigured; abide in Him, and He shall abide in you.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

**Spurgeon:** applies the principle to modern “idols” too — the god of modern thought is the creation of the thinker himself, evolved out of his own consciousness. A god fashioned by our own thoughts is no more a God than an image made by our hands. “The true God must of necessity be his own revealer.” — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Gill:** notes that some versions (LXX, Vulgate, Targum) render this as a petition: “let them that make them be like unto them” — i.e., let them be given up to a reprobate mind (cf. Rom. 1:28). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

---

## Verses 9–11

**“O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield. O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield. You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield.”**

**Traditional reading — three concentric groups:** (1) Israel — the lay people generally; (2) the house of Aaron — the priests; (3) those who fear the LORD — understood by most commentators as Gentile proselytes or “God-fearers” who honoured Israel’s God without becoming Jews (cf. Acts 10:1–2; 13:16, 26). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

**Liturgical arrangement:** Ellicott suggests that one officiating priest addressed each group with “trust in Jehovah,” and the full choir took up the refrain, “He is their help and shield.” The crash of the triple choral answer “comes with magnificent effect.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/115.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-115.html

**Spurgeon** on the priests: “You who are nearest to him, trust him most; your very calling is connected with his truth and is meant to declare his glory, therefore never entertain a doubt concerning him, but lead the way in holy confidence.” — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Pulpit Commentary** differs slightly on the third group: it sees a climax — first ordinary Israelites, next those officially holy (priests), finally those actually holy (the truly faithful Israelites) — rather than proselytes. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

**Gill:** interprets “you who fear the LORD” as proselytes following Jarchi (the medieval Jewish commentator), noting the distinction in Acts 13:26 between “the people of the Jews” and “those who fear God.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

---

## Verses 12–13

**“The LORD is mindful of us; He will bless us. He will bless the house of Israel; He will bless the house of Aaron; He will bless those who fear the LORD—small and great alike.”**

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist draws on God’s past faithfulness as confidence for future blessing. “God hath, and therefore God will, is an ordinary Scripture argument” (Trapp, cited by Guzik). The same three groups addressed in vv. 9–11 now receive the assurance of blessing. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

The small are mentioned first — meaning the insignificant will not be forgotten. “God’s blessing is for you, whoever you may be, if you will only stop trusting in yourself … and instead begin to trust God” (Boice, cited by Guzik). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Spurgeon: “It is his nature to bless, it is his prerogative to bless, it is his glory to bless, it is his delight to bless; he has promised to bless, and therefore be sure of this, that he will bless and bless and bless without ceasing.” — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**The Expositor’s Bible Commentary:** suggests that vv. 12–15 were sung by priests or Levites as authoritative assurances from commissioned lips — “Jehovah’s response to Israel’s obedience to the preceding summons … swiftly sent, as His answers ever are.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-115.html

---

## Verses 14–15

**“May the LORD give you increase, both you and your children. May you be blessed by the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.”**

**Traditional reading:** In the ancient world, many looked to idols for fertility and prosperity. The psalmist counters that Yahweh is the true source of increase — extending even to one’s children. The blessing is pronounced by “the Maker of heaven and earth,” again exalting Yahweh above all idols. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

The Pulpit Commentary links “increase” to the original Abrahamic blessing (Gen. 13:16; 17:4–6), noting that the main fulfilment came through the conversion of the Gentiles — but even the lineal descendants of Abraham have increased “to an extent which is most extraordinary.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

**On a possible “prosperity” reading:** No source I found among the searched sites applies this text in a “prosperity gospel” or “Word of Faith” framework. The traditional reading treats the increase as primarily covenantal — numbers, spiritual blessing, and God’s provision — not as a guarantee of individual wealth. Guzik notes that the blessing flows from trusting the Creator, as a contrast to looking to pagan idols for fertility and prosperity. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

---

## Verse 16

**“The highest heavens belong to the LORD, but the earth He has given to mankind.”**

**Traditional reading:** God’s authority as Creator extends over both heaven and earth. The heavens — in all three biblical senses (the sky, the starry realm, and God’s dwelling place) — belong specifically to the LORD. The earth He has entrusted to humanity, recalling the dominion grant in Genesis 1:26–30. This implies stewardship, not ownership: “We can use, but we should not waste and destroy” (Guzik). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Maclaren (cited by Guzik): “The earth is man’s, but by Jehovah’s gift. Therefore its inhabitants should remember the terms of their tenure, and thankfully recognise His giving love.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Kidner (cited by Guzik): “All is his, but we are his substantial heirs and trustees. There is generosity in the phrase, ‘the earth he has given’; there is responsibility as well … Behind the gift is the Giver.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

**Gill** adds that God has not left the earth entirely to men’s care, as if He had no concern in it. Men are at most stewards and deputies under Him, accountable for their use of it. He also notes Maimonides’ philosophical reading: God alone perfectly knows the truth of the heavens; to man He has given understanding of what is under the heavens. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

**Pulpit Commentary:** God framed this world for man and adapted it with minutest care — “certainly not least for his own people, who are ‘the salt of the earth’ — the human race by representation.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

---

## Verse 17

**“It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence.”**

This verse is one where Protestant traditions offer different nuances, and where the Old Testament’s view of the afterlife is debated.

**Traditional reading (majority evangelical view):** The dead cannot praise God *on earth among the living*. Their voice is no longer heard in the earthly congregation. The verse is not a denial of an afterlife; it describes the observable reality that the grave is silent, and therefore the living must seize the opportunity to praise God now. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/ ; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Gill** is explicit: “The souls of departed saints can and do praise the Lord: these die not with their bodies, nor sleep in the grave; they go immediately to God and Christ … particularly in praising him.” However, “they cannot praise him with their bodily organs until the resurrection.” He also notes that some distinguish two groups in the verse: the “dead” (spiritually dead idol-worshippers, like their idols) and “any that go down into silence” (the physically dead). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/115.htm

**StudyLight.org** also insists this verse has been misused “to support the opinion that the Old Testament saints were in the dark on the subject of immortality. The whole text goes to prove the very opposite.” It points to Ps. 16:9–11; 17:15; 49:15; 73:23–24; and Isa. 26:19 as evidence that the Hebrews did believe in an afterlife. “Forevermore” (v. 18) is “a word of very frequent use; and it has but one meaning, and that meaning is Eternity.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/115-17.html

**Spurgeon:** says the psalmist’s point is that since “those who were dead and gone could no longer sing psalms unto the Lord among the sons of men, he exhorts the faithful who were then living to take care that God is not robbed of his praise.” — https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps115.php

**Ellicott** takes a less resolved view: the psalmist is “struck with the dreadful thought that death broke the covenant relationship, and silenced prayer and praise.” He wonders whether the sight of the slain after a victory prompted the verse — those who helped win the triumph could not share in the praises ascending to Jehovah. The LXX translates “silence” as “Hades.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/115.htm

**NET Bible notes:** simply note that “silence” is “a metonymy here for death (see Ps 94:17).” — https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Psa%20115:17,18

**Pulpit Commentary:** “The mention of ‘heaven and earth’ (v. 15) reminds them of the third place — Sheol. In Sheol is no praise of God, but only ‘silence.’” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/115.htm

**Summary of the difference:** Reformed/evangelical teachers (Spurgeon, Gill, Guzik) read the verse as referring to the cessation of *earthly* praise — the dead cannot join the earthly congregation — while affirming that the souls of the righteous do praise God in heaven, and that bodily praise will be restored at the resurrection. Older critical commentators (Ellicott, Pulpit) tend to read it more straightforwardly as reflecting an older, less developed view of Sheol where all conscious activity ceases — though even they acknowledge that the final verse pushes beyond this with “forevermore.”

---

## Verse 18

**“But it is we who will bless the LORD, both now and forevermore. Hallelujah!”**

**Traditional reading:** The living take up the responsibility to ensure God’s praise does not cease on earth. “From this time forth and forevermore” may have the double sense of *in this life and the life to come*. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

Spurgeon: “We who are still living will take care that the praises of God shall not fail among the sons of men. Our afflictions and depressions of spirit shall not cause us to suspend our praises.” If the praise is to last forevermore, “then it does extend into the world to come.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik) connects this back to Jesus in the upper room: “the Singer Whose deepest passion was ever the will of God and the glory of His name; … the One Who was soon going into the silence where no note of praise would be heard; and yet to the One Who would turn the silence into song forevermore.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

**Spurgeon’s closing:** “Though the dead cannot, and the wicked will not, and the careless do not praise God, yet we will shout ‘Hallelujah’ for ever and ever. Amen.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-115/

---

## Summary of Key Distinctives Found

**Reformed (Spurgeon, Gill):** Heavy emphasis on divine sovereignty (v. 3), the spiritual law that we become like what we worship (v. 8), and the covenant faithfulness of God. Gill ties nearly every verse back to the doctrines of grace — election, effectual calling, perseverance.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasises personal application, the role of the Holy Spirit, and reads the psalm through the lens of Christ singing it at the Last Supper. Guzik draws strong connections to the New Testament and to Christian living.

**Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit, Cambridge):** Focus on liturgical structure, historical context, and choral arrangement. Ellicott and Pulpit tend toward a more academic, sometimes critical approach (e.g., on Sheol and the dating of the psalm).

**On the afterlife question (v. 17):** All evangelical sources reject the claim that OT saints had no hope of eternal life. Gill, Guzik, and Spurgeon all affirm conscious existence after death. The older critical commentators (Ellicott, Pulpit) are more willing to see the verse as reflecting a stage in the development of Israel’s understanding of the afterlife.

**Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist, and prosperity-gospel perspectives:** I was unable to access dedicated sources from these traditions within the search limits. No material from the allowed Catholic/Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) or Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) appeared in the search results, and no prosperity-gospel reading of this psalm surfaced on the searched sites.
